before: In 1910 a preacher in Chicago began to teach something different. William H. Durham (1873-1912) led the North Avenue Mission, which became a center of Pentecostal teaching in the Midwest. He had received the baptism of the Spirit with tongues at Azusa Street in 1907. But he had come to believe that the Holiness doctrine of a second crisis of sanctification was not in the Bible.

Durham preached the "Finished Work of Calvary." He taught that at the cross Christ finished the work of redemption, and that a believer receives sanctification at conversion, when he is placed "in Christ." After this, the believer grows in holiness by faith and by the Spirit throughout life. In Durham's view the believer has only two crisis experiences: new birth and baptism in the Spirit. His main texts were these: "For by one offering He has perfected forever those who are being sanctified" (Hebrews 10:14), and "But of Him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God--and righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1 Corinthians 1:30). He also pointed to Romans 6:11: "Likewise you also, reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord."

before: Many Pentecostal ministers, especially in the American Midwest and Southwest, held the Finished Work position and wanted a fellowship. In April 1914 a General Council met at Hot Springs, Arkansas. E. N. Bell was elected as its first chairman and J. Roswell Flower as its secretary. The delegates formed the General Council of the Assemblies of God. Their goals were practical and spiritual: to cooperate in missions, to recognize ministers, to protect doctrine, and to preserve the Pentecostal witness.

before: **The three appear together.** At the baptism of Jesus the Son stands in the water, "the Spirit of God" descends "like a dove," and a voice from heaven says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:16-17). One God in one person could not do all three at once without confusion.
after: **The Father, Son, and Spirit are presented distinctly.** At Jesus’ baptism, the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends "like a dove," and the Father’s voice says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:16-17). Trinitarians understand this and other passages to reveal one God eternally existing as three distinct persons, not merely three titles or temporary roles. Oneness Pentecostals interpret these passages differently; state their position in terms its adherents would recognize before explaining why this course rejects it.

before: Early Pentecostals at first distrusted denominations, but practical needs and the example of the apostolic church led them to organize. Holiness Pentecostal bodies, such as the Church of God (Cleveland), the Pentecostal Holiness Church and the Church of God in Christ, taught three works of grace: new birth, entire sanctification and Spirit baptism. In 1910 William H. Durham taught the Finished Work of Calvary, in which sanctification begins at conversion and grows through life, and many ministers who agreed formed the Assemblies of God at Hot Springs in 1914. In 1913 at Arroyo Seco, a teaching arose that baptism should be in the name of Jesus only, and it grew into the Oneness view, which holds that God is one person and not three. The Assemblies of God adopted its Statement of Fundamental Truths in 1916, and classical Pentecostals have answered Oneness teaching from Matthew 3, Matthew 28 and John 14. We state differences openly, hold the Trinity firmly and keep the unity of the Spirit.

Holiness Pentecostal bodies, such as the Church of God (Cleveland), the Pentecostal Holiness Church and the Church of God in Christ, taught three works of grace: new birth, entire sanctification and Spirit baptism. In 1910 William H. Durham taught the Finished Work of Calvary, in which sanctification begins at conversion and grows through life, and many ministers who agreed formed the Assemblies of God at Hot Springs in 1914. In 1913–1916, a baptismal controversy developed into the Oneness view, which rejects the classical Trinitarian distinction of three divine persons and teaches that the one God is revealed in Jesus Christ. Trinitarian Pentecostals disagree with this account of God, while recognizing Oneness believers as fellow Pentecostals in the broader historical movement.
